name: Personal Finance
notes: Competency areas and item counts come from the 2025-2026 FBLA Competitive Events Guidelines, Personal Finance (updated Nov 2025), Study Guide: Knowledge Areas and Objectives: https://www.pafbla.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Personal-Finance.pdf. The guide lists six areas with test-item counts (20/15/5/5/50/5, total 100), and those counts are used as the sub weights. The guideline notes sample items are in CONNECT (members only), so questions were written from the objectives, not copied. Dollar amounts are US federal rules, and the tax items avoid year-specific limits. Chart labels on the guideline PDF did not match the study guide counts, so the study guide was followed.

questions.q: Which form of payment draws funds directly from the payer's checking account at the time of purchase?
questions.explain: A debit card pulls money from the cardholder's own deposit account at the point of sale. A credit card borrows from the issuer.

questions.q: Which function of money allows prices of goods and services to be stated and compared?
questions.explain: Money serves as a unit of measure (common yardstick) so prices can be compared. Medium of exchange is what is used to pay.

questions.q: A shopkeeper accepts a $20 bill because every other merchant also accepts it for goods. Which function of money does this best illustrate?
questions.explain: Money as a medium of exchange is accepted widely in trade. The trap is store of value, which concerns keeping purchasing power over time.

questions.q: Which statement about the time value of money is correct?
choices: A dollar received today is worth less than a dollar received next year when interest rates are positive.
A dollar received today is worth the same as a dollar received next year, regardless of interest rates.
Money received in the future is worth more than the same amount today, because of inflation.
A dollar received today can be invested to grow, so it is worth more than the same dollar received later.
questions.explain: Money on hand today can earn interest, so it has greater value than the same amount received later. The other choices reverse or ignore this relationship.

questions.q: What is the main difference between a debit card and a credit card?
choices: Credit cards draw from a checking account, while debit cards are loans.
Debit cards always charge interest on purchases.
Debit cards require a credit check before approval.
Debit cards withdraw funds from the cardholder's own bank account, while credit cards borrow from the issuer.
questions.explain: Debit spends the cardholder's own money. Credit creates a debt owed to the card issuer.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of passive income?
choices: Hourly wages for a full-time job
Rental income from a property leased to tenants
questions.explain: Passive income comes from assets or arrangements that do not require ongoing work, such as rent. Wages, commissions and tips all require labour.

questions.q: A salesperson earns a base salary of $30,000 plus 5% commission on sales. Which describes this pay structure?
choices: A combination of salary and incentive pay
questions.explain: The base salary is fixed pay, and the commission is incentive pay tied to performance.

questions.q: An employee earns $1,200 gross pay for a pay period. Federal and state income tax withholding plus FICA total $270. What is net pay for the period?
questions.explain: Net pay equals gross pay minus withholdings: $1,200 minus $270 is $930. The trap is $1,000, which subtracts only part of the withholdings.

questions.q: Which document is a written order instructing a bank to pay a specific amount from the payer's account?
questions.explain: A check is a negotiable instrument directing the bank to pay the payee from the drawer's account.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT currency in circulation?
questions.explain: Treasury bonds are government debt securities, not money in circulation. The other items are legal currency.

questions.q: Which best describes the purpose of consumer credit?
choices: Letting a consumer buy goods or services now and repay later, usually with interest
Permanently transferring ownership of savings to a lender
Guaranteeing a fixed return on investments
Protecting the consumer against identity theft
questions.explain: Credit lets consumers use goods or services before paying, in exchange for interest or fees.

questions.q: Which U.S. federal law requires lenders to disclose the APR and finance charges on consumer credit?
questions.explain: The Truth in Lending Act (Regulation Z) requires standardized credit cost disclosures. The FCRA covers credit reports.

questions.q: Which U.S. federal agency was created after the 2008 financial crisis to enforce most consumer financial protection laws?
questions.explain: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau was created by the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010 to supervise consumer financial products.

questions.q: A consumer's debit card is lost and the loss is reported within two business days. What is the maximum liability under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act?
questions.explain: Under the EFTA, reporting within two business days caps liability at $50. Reporting later raises the cap to $500.

questions.q: A $1,000 deposit earns 5% interest compounded annually. What is its value after one year?
questions.explain: $1,000 times 1.05 equals $1,050. The trap is adding 5% of the deposit incorrectly or using the wrong base.

questions.q: Under the Fair Credit Billing Act, how many days does a consumer generally have to send a written notice of a billing error after the first statement showing it?
questions.explain: The FCBA gives 60 days to dispute a billing error in writing after the first statement with the error is sent.

questions.q: What does the store-of-value function of money mean?
choices: Money keeps its purchasing worth over time so it can be saved for later use
Money is used to measure the price of goods
Money is accepted by sellers in exchange for goods
Money is issued by private companies
questions.explain: Store of value means money can be saved and used later without losing its worth, though inflation erodes it.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-cash employee benefit?
questions.explain: Health insurance paid by the employer is a fringe benefit, not cash compensation.

questions.q: Which term describes income before any taxes or deductions are subtracted?
questions.explain: Gross income is the total before taxes and deductions. Net income and take-home pay are after them.

questions.q: Which is an example of an electronic funds transfer?
choices: Writing a personal check to a landlord
Paying for groceries with a debit card at point of sale
Depositing cash at a teller window
Buying a money order at a post office
questions.explain: A debit card purchase moves funds electronically from the account at the point of sale. The other options involve paper or cash.

questions.q: Which step should come first in the financial planning process?
questions.explain: Goals guide every later decision, so they come first in the planning process.

questions.q: Which of these is a short-term financial goal?
choices: Saving for a vacation in six months
Funding a child's college in 18 years
questions.explain: Short-term goals are typically achievable within about one year. The others are long-term.

questions.q: Which formula is used to calculate net worth?
questions.explain: Net worth equals what you own minus what you owe. Adding liabilities instead of subtracting them is a common error.

questions.q: A monthly budget shows after-tax income of $4,000, fixed expenses of $2,600, and planned variable expenses of $1,500. What is the result?
questions.explain: Total expenses are $4,100, so the budget runs $100 short. The trap is forgetting variable expenses.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of an emergency fund?
choices: Covering unexpected expenses such as job loss or medical bills
questions.explain: An emergency fund is a reserve of liquid savings for unplanned events.

questions.q: A common guideline for the size of an emergency fund is:
choices: Three to six months of living expenses
questions.explain: Financial educators commonly recommend three to six months of living expenses in an accessible account.

questions.q: Which budgeting method assigns every dollar of income to a category until none is left unassigned?
questions.explain: In zero-based budgeting, income minus planned spending equals zero. The 50/30/20 rule is a percentage guideline, not a zero-balance plan.

questions.q: Which expense is a fixed expense?
questions.explain: Fixed expenses stay the same each period. Rent is usually set by a lease.

questions.q: Which financial statement lists assets, liabilities, and equity at a single point in time?
questions.explain: A balance sheet is a snapshot at one date. Income and cash flow statements cover a period.

questions.q: Which of the following is a long-term financial goal?
choices: Paying a parking ticket this week
questions.explain: Long-term goals are typically more than five years away.

questions.q: Which list correctly describes the SMART goal criteria?
questions.explain: SMART stands for specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

questions.q: Which action most directly increases a person's net worth?
choices: Paying a $200 restaurant bill with a credit card
Saving $500 from a paycheck in a savings account
Spending $500 of savings on a trip
questions.explain: Saving income adds to assets with no offsetting liability. Borrowing or spending from savings does not raise net worth.

questions.q: Which of these is a sinking fund?
choices: Saving a fixed amount each month for an annual insurance premium
A standby credit line for emergencies
A money market account used for daily spending
questions.explain: A sinking fund sets aside money regularly for a known future expense.

questions.q: Which best describes a budget?
choices: A list of past transactions only
A plan showing how income will be spent and saved
A loan agreement with a lender
questions.explain: A budget is a forward-looking plan for income, spending and saving.

questions.q: An employer's 401(k) match is best classified as:
choices: A fringe benefit that supports retirement saving
questions.explain: An employer match is a non-wage benefit that supports retirement saving.

questions.q: Which provider is a depository institution that accepts deposits and makes loans to consumers and businesses?
questions.explain: Commercial banks take deposits and lend. Brokers and insurance agents do not hold deposits.

questions.q: Which description best fits a credit union?
choices: A for-profit corporation owned by shareholders
A government agency that sets interest rates
An investment bank that underwrites stock offerings
questions.explain: Credit unions are cooperatives owned by their members and return earnings to them as lower fees and better rates.

questions.q: Which provider is a broker-dealer that executes trades in securities for clients?
questions.explain: Brokerage firms buy and sell securities on behalf of clients.

questions.q: When choosing a bank, which check matters most for protecting your deposits?
choices: Whether deposits are insured by the FDIC
The size of its advertising budget
questions.explain: FDIC insurance protects deposits up to the legal limit if an insured bank fails.

questions.q: A consumer compares a payday loan with a credit union small-dollar loan. Which factor most clearly favours the credit union?
choices: A fee of $15 for every $100 borrowed
A requirement to post a post-dated check
A lower interest rate with repayment over several months
questions.explain: Payday loans are short, high-cost loans due in full on the next payday. Longer, lower-rate installment terms are the clearest advantage.

questions.q: Which type of investment represents ownership in a company?
questions.explain: Common stock gives shareholders an ownership stake. Bonds are debt.

questions.q: A bond pays $50 per year in interest on a $1,000 face value. What is its coupon rate?
questions.explain: Coupon rate equals annual interest divided by face value: $50 divided by $1,000 is 5%.

questions.q: Which investment is generally considered the least risky?
questions.explain: Treasury bills are backed by the U.S. government and carry very low default risk.

questions.q: Which factor is most important when selecting investments for a goal five years away?
choices: Putting the entire amount into a single stock
Expecting guaranteed returns in all cases
Matching the investment to the time horizon and risk tolerance
questions.explain: The time horizon and risk tolerance determine how much volatility an investor can absorb.

questions.q: What does diversification mean?
choices: Putting all money into one investment
Spreading investments across different assets to reduce risk
questions.explain: Diversification reduces the impact of any single investment's loss.

questions.q: Which statement about marginal tax rates is correct?
choices: Each dollar of income is taxed at one flat rate.
The top bracket's rate applies to all income once you reach it.
Only the portion of income within a bracket is taxed at that bracket's rate.
Tax brackets apply only to capital gains.
questions.explain: A progressive system taxes each bracket's slice of income at that bracket's rate. Higher income does not raise the rate on earlier dollars.

questions.q: On a pay stub, which item represents the employee's share of Social Security and Medicare taxes?
questions.explain: FICA covers Social Security and Medicare. Employers match the amount.

questions.q: Gross pay is $2,000 and total withholdings are $460. What is net pay?
questions.explain: Net pay is $2,000 minus $460, which equals $1,540.

questions.q: On a check, what is the payee line?
choices: The person or business receiving the payment
The date the check was written
questions.explain: The payee is the person or business that receives the money.

questions.q: What must match when you write a check?
choices: The amount in numerals and in words
questions.explain: The numerical and written amounts should agree to avoid disputes or altered checks.

questions.q: A check shows $250 in numerals but the written amount reads two hundred fifty-five dollars. Which amount generally controls?
choices: The amount shown on the bank statement
The average of the two amounts
questions.explain: Under the Uniform Commercial Code, the written words generally control over numerals when they conflict.

questions.q: Your checkbook balance is $1,200. The bank statement shows $1,350, with an outstanding check of $200 and an unrecorded $50 service fee. What is the adjusted balance?
questions.explain: Bank side: $1,350 minus $200 is $1,150. Book side: $1,200 minus the $50 fee is $1,150. Both match.

questions.q: Generally, how long should you keep federal tax returns and supporting records?
choices: At least three years from the filing date
questions.explain: The IRS generally has three years to audit, so three years is the usual minimum. Some situations require longer.

questions.q: Which record is most useful for tracking where money was spent during a month?
questions.explain: A transaction register records each deposit, withdrawal and payment in order.

questions.q: To deduct a charitable cash gift of $250 or more on a federal return, what is generally required?
choices: A written acknowledgment from the charity
A notarized letter from the donor
questions.explain: The IRS requires a contemporaneous written acknowledgment from the charity for single cash gifts of $250 or more.

questions.q: A single filer has a $15,000 standard deduction and itemized deductions of $12,000. Which is more beneficial?
choices: Itemize and reduce taxable income by $12,000
Take both the standard deduction and itemize
Itemize and add $3,000 to taxable income
questions.explain: Taxpayers generally take whichever is larger, and the larger one here is the standard deduction. Itemizing and standard deduction cannot be combined.

questions.q: Which is the safest practice for managing online bank accounts?
choices: Using the same password for every site
Saving login details on a public computer
questions.explain: Multi-factor authentication stops most account takeovers even if a password is stolen.

questions.q: A $1,000 credit card balance carries 18% APR charged monthly (1.5% per month) with no new purchases. What is the first month's interest?
questions.explain: The monthly rate is 18% divided by 12, or 1.5%. Applied to $1,000, the interest is $15. The trap is using $18, the annual rate in dollars.

questions.q: Why do cardholders pay interest on credit cards?
choices: The issuer waives interest after 30 days
The cardholder pays the full statement balance each month
The cardholder carries a balance past the grace period
The card carries an annual fee
questions.explain: Interest starts when a balance is carried past the grace period. Paying the full statement balance usually avoids interest on purchases.

questions.q: A $3,000 balance at 24% APR requires a $60 minimum payment. Why does the balance fall so slowly?
choices: The minimum is applied entirely to principal
The issuer refunds interest each month
Interest applies only to new purchases
Most of the minimum covers accrued interest, leaving little for principal
questions.explain: Monthly interest is $3,000 times 2%, or $60, so the entire minimum goes to interest.

questions.q: Which is a common warning sign of identity theft?
choices: Receiving a monthly statement you expected
A credit score that rose slightly
A credit card bill for purchases you did not make
questions.explain: Unfamiliar charges or accounts are a key sign. Expected statements and normal scores are not warnings.

questions.q: Under U.S. federal law, how often can a consumer get a free credit report from each nationwide credit bureau?
questions.explain: The Fair Credit Reporting Act entitles consumers to a free report from each nationwide bureau every 12 months.

questions.q: Which factor has the largest impact on a FICO score?
questions.explain: Payment history is the largest factor, at about 35 percent. Income is not used in scoring.

questions.q: Which statement about the credit utilization ratio is correct?
choices: It is total card balances divided by total credit limits, and lower is generally better
Higher ratios generally improve a credit score
It is calculated from the borrower's income
questions.explain: Utilization is revolving balances divided by limits. Keeping it low generally helps the score.

questions.q: What is the best first step before taking on a new loan?
choices: Compare the total cost, including interest
questions.explain: Comparing total cost, including interest and fees, shows what the loan really costs.

questions.q: What is the principal of a loan?
choices: The original amount borrowed, excluding interest
questions.explain: Principal is the amount borrowed. Interest and fees are separate charges.

questions.q: Which debt-repayment method pays off the smallest balance first?
questions.explain: The snowball method targets the smallest balance for quick wins. The avalanche method targets the highest rate.

questions.q: Using the avalanche method, which debt should receive extra payments first? Card A: $2,000 at 22%. Card B: $5,000 at 15%. Car loan: $8,000 at 6%.
questions.explain: The avalanche method targets the highest interest rate first, which is Card A at 22%.

questions.q: Which bill is most important to pay on time to avoid losing housing?
questions.explain: Missing rent or mortgage payments can lead to eviction or foreclosure, so it takes priority.

questions.q: Which U.S. federal law restricts how third-party debt collectors may contact consumers?
questions.explain: The FDCPA limits collector contact times and methods and bans harassment and false statements.

questions.q: Which retirement plan allows employees to contribute pre-tax income through payroll deduction?
questions.explain: Traditional 401(k) contributions reduce current taxable wages, and withdrawals in retirement are taxed as income.

questions.q: Which statement about a Roth IRA is correct?
choices: Contributions are tax-deductible in the year made
Withdrawals of contributions are taxed as ordinary income
Required minimum distributions begin at age 25
Contributions use after-tax dollars, and qualified retirement withdrawals are tax-free
questions.explain: Roth contributions are made with after-tax money, and qualified withdrawals are tax-free. Contributions can be withdrawn without tax at any time.

questions.q: Which form does a student complete to apply for federal financial aid?
questions.explain: The Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) is required for federal grants and loans.

questions.q: Which type of education funding generally does NOT have to be repaid?
questions.explain: Pell Grants are need-based grants that do not need repayment. All the loan options must be repaid.

questions.q: Which document names a person who can manage finances if the owner becomes incapacitated?
questions.explain: A durable power of attorney stays in effect if the principal becomes incapacitated. A living will covers medical care.

questions.q: Which is a key advantage of a revocable living trust over a will?
choices: It can avoid probate for assets titled in the trust
It eliminates all estate taxes automatically
questions.explain: Assets titled in the trust pass outside probate. A revocable trust can be changed, and it does not automatically remove estate tax.

questions.q: Which form does an employer send to an employee to report annual wages and withholding?
questions.explain: Form W-2 reports wages and taxes withheld. Form 1099 is used for non-employee income.

questions.q: Which filing status generally offers the largest standard deduction?
questions.explain: Married filing jointly generally has the largest standard deduction, which is double the single amount.

questions.q: Which tax item reduces tax owed dollar for dollar?
questions.explain: A credit reduces tax directly. A deduction only reduces taxable income.

questions.q: A taxpayer in the 22% bracket has $1,000 of additional taxable income, all in that bracket. How much additional federal income tax is owed?
questions.explain: Tax is 22% of $1,000, which is $220. The trap is treating the rate as 2.2 times the amount.

questions.q: Which tax is paid on the value of goods and services at the point of purchase?
questions.explain: Sales tax is collected at the register on the taxable price of goods and services.

questions.q: Which agency collects federal income tax?
questions.explain: The IRS administers and collects federal income taxes.

questions.q: Which statement about capital gains is correct?
choices: A capital gain is a loss on a sold asset
Short-term gains are always taxed at a lower rate than long-term gains
Long-term gains on assets held more than one year generally get lower rates than ordinary income
Capital gains are never subject to federal tax
questions.explain: Assets held more than one year usually qualify for lower long-term rates. Short-term gains are taxed as ordinary income.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a traditional IRA?
choices: Contributions are taxed upfront and withdrawals are tax-free
Earnings are taxed each year as they accrue
No contributions are allowed after age 30
Contributions may be deductible, and retirement withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income
questions.explain: Traditional IRA earnings grow tax-deferred. Contributions may be deductible, and withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income.

questions.q: Which U.S. federal law protects consumers against unfair practices in credit reporting?
questions.explain: The FCRA governs how credit bureaus collect, share and correct consumer credit information.

questions.q: Which law prohibits credit discrimination based on race, sex, or marital status?
questions.explain: The ECOA prohibits credit discrimination on several protected bases, including race, sex and marital status.

questions.q: Which statement about a secured loan is correct?
choices: It always has a higher rate than unsecured loans
It is available only to businesses
It is backed by collateral the lender can seize on default
questions.explain: A secured loan is backed by collateral, such as a car or home. Rates are often lower, not higher.

questions.q: A borrower defaults on a car loan. Under the Uniform Commercial Code, what is the lender's typical remedy?
choices: Repossess the collateral after giving required notice
Collect from the borrower's employer without notice
questions.explain: A secured lender may repossess collateral after default, subject to notice rules under the UCC.

questions.q: Which action best protects against identity theft?
choices: Posting your Social Security number on social media
Placing a credit freeze with each credit bureau
Banking on public Wi-Fi without protection
questions.explain: A credit freeze blocks new credit checks, so thieves cannot open accounts in your name.

questions.q: What is a fraud alert on a credit report?
choices: A permanent block on all credit
A notice asking creditors to verify identity before opening new credit, lasting one year
questions.explain: An initial fraud alert lasts one year and asks lenders to take extra steps to verify identity. It does not block all credit.

questions.q: Which statement describes a credit freeze?
choices: It lasts seven years and cannot be lifted
It prevents you from getting your own credit report
It applies only to business credit
It restricts access to your credit report so new accounts are harder to open, and it is free to place and lift
questions.explain: Under U.S. law, freezes are free and can be lifted or placed at each bureau. You can still see your own report.

questions.q: A debt collector threatens arrest for unpaid debt. What is the most appropriate first step?
choices: Request written validation of the debt under the FDCPA
Give the collector your online banking password
questions.explain: Debt collectors cannot threaten arrest for civil debt. Requesting written validation is the consumer's right under the FDCPA.

questions.q: What does a Form W-4 tell an employer?
choices: How much to claim as a refund
Where to file an estate return
How much federal income tax to withhold
questions.explain: Form W-4 sets the employee's federal withholding based on filing status and adjustments.

questions.q: Which is a common purpose of Form 1099?
questions.explain: Form 1099 series reports income such as freelance pay, interest and dividends. Wages use Form W-2.

questions.q: Which record-keeping practice best supports a tax audit?
choices: Keeping receipts and statements for the required period, generally three years
Shredding all statements after one month
Storing records only on a phone
questions.explain: Documentation is the basis for supporting deductions and income. Keeping it for the required period protects the taxpayer.

questions.q: Which term describes the amount a policyholder pays out of pocket before insurance begins to pay?
questions.explain: The deductible is the out-of-pocket amount before the insurer pays. The premium is the regular cost of coverage.

questions.q: What is a premium in insurance?
choices: The amount paid to keep an insurance policy in force
The amount the insurer pays on a claim
The maximum payout under the policy
A fee paid to an insurance agent
questions.explain: The premium is the price of coverage, usually paid monthly or annually.

questions.q: Which insurance protects against liability for injuries you cause to others?
choices: Collision coverage on your own car
questions.explain: Liability coverage pays for legal defence and damages you owe to third parties.

questions.q: Which strategy transfers risk to another party?
questions.explain: Insurance transfers the financial risk of a loss to the insurer in exchange for a premium. Avoidance and reduction change the risk itself.

questions.q: What is coinsurance in an insurance policy?
choices: The insurer pays 100% of covered costs after the premium is paid
The insured pays a fixed monthly amount regardless of claims
The insurer pays nothing until the policy limit is reached
The insured pays a set percentage of covered costs after the deductible is met
questions.explain: Coinsurance is the insured's share of covered costs after the deductible, such as 20 percent. It is not a fixed fee.

vocab.def: Any transfer of money made electronically rather than by cash or paper check, such as a debit card purchase or direct deposit.
A payment card that withdraws funds directly from the cardholder's deposit account at the time of purchase.
A payment card that lets the holder borrow from the issuer up to a credit limit and repay later, usually with interest.
A written order directing a bank to pay a specific amount from the drawer's account to the payee.
The function of money as a widely accepted means of paying for goods and services.
The function of money as a way to save purchasing power for future use.
The function of money as a common yardstick for stating and comparing the prices of goods and services.
Total income earned before taxes, withholdings and other deductions are subtracted.
Income remaining after taxes and deductions have been subtracted from gross income.
The principle that money available now is worth more than the same amount in the future because it can earn interest.
Currency that a government requires creditors to accept as payment for debts.
Money, goods or services provided to a consumer with the agreement to repay later, usually with interest or fees.
Total assets minus total liabilities, showing what a person owns after paying off what is owed.
A plan that projects income and expenses for a period and shows how money will be spent and saved.
A budgeting method in which every dollar of income is assigned to a category so that income minus planned spending equals zero.
A reserve of easily accessible savings set aside for unexpected expenses or loss of income.
Money set aside regularly over time to pay for a known future expense.
An expense that stays about the same each period, such as rent or a loan payment.
An expense that changes from period to period, such as groceries, fuel or entertainment.
A financial goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
A saving approach in which a set amount is moved into savings or investments as soon as income is received, before other spending.
A depository institution that accepts deposits and makes loans to consumers and businesses.
A member-owned, not-for-profit financial cooperative that offers deposit and lending services to its members.
A firm that buys and sells securities on behalf of clients, often as a broker-dealer.
A business that lends money in exchange for personal property held as collateral, which is returned if the loan and fee are repaid.
A short-term, high-cost loan due in full on the borrower's next payday, often with very high effective annual rates.
A person or firm legally required to act in the best interest of the client when giving financial advice or managing assets.
A security that represents an ownership share in a corporation and may pay dividends and carry voting rights.
A debt security in which the investor lends money to an issuer in exchange for periodic interest and repayment of principal at maturity.
The annual interest paid on a bond expressed as a percentage of its face value.
Spreading investments across different assets so that a loss in one holding has less effect on the whole portfolio.
A short-term U.S. government debt security sold at a discount and repaid at face value at maturity.
A pooled investment vehicle that holds a diversified portfolio of securities managed on behalf of many investors.
The tax rate applied to the next dollar of taxable income, which rises through progressive brackets.
Payroll taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare, withheld from employee pay and matched by employers.
The amount an employee actually receives after all taxes and deductions are withheld from gross pay.
The IRS form an employee completes so the employer knows how much federal income tax to withhold from pay.
An IRS information return reporting income paid to a person who is not an employee, such as freelance pay or interest.
The process of comparing the bank statement with the checkbook record and adjusting for outstanding checks, deposits in transit and fees.
The yearly cost of borrowing expressed as a percentage, including interest and certain fees, as required under the Truth in Lending Act.
The share of available revolving credit in use, calculated as total card balances divided by total credit limits.
A notice on a credit report, lasting one year for an initial alert, asking lenders to verify identity before opening new credit.
A restriction placed with each credit bureau that blocks access to a credit report, at no cost, until it is lifted.
A debt repayment method that pays the smallest balance first while making minimum payments on the others.
A debt repayment method that directs extra payments to the debt with the highest interest rate first.
A loan backed by collateral that the lender can seize if the borrower defaults.
A retirement account funded with after-tax contributions in which qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free.
The profit from selling an asset for more than its purchase price, taxed at rates that depend on how long it was held.
An amount that reduces the tax owed dollar for dollar, unlike a deduction, which only reduces taxable income.
A need-based federal grant for undergraduate students that does not have to be repaid.
A trust the owner can change during life that holds assets, allowing them to pass outside probate at death.
The Free Application for Federal Student Aid, required to apply for federal grants, work-study and loans.
A federal law that limits how third-party debt collectors may contact consumers and bans abusive or deceptive practices.
The periodic amount paid to an insurer to keep an insurance policy in force.
The amount the policyholder must pay out of pocket on a covered loss before the insurer begins to pay.
The percentage of covered costs the insured pays after the deductible is met, with the insurer paying the rest.
Coverage that pays legal defence costs and damages owed to others for injury or property damage the insured causes.
A risk management strategy of not engaging in an activity that could cause a loss.
A risk management strategy of shifting the financial burden of a possible loss to another party, usually through insurance or a contract.
Accepting a risk and paying any resulting loss from one's own funds, either deliberately or because the risk is too small to insure.
